title: Arrays & Associative Arrays
summary: Bash arrays are underused and misunderstood. Indexed arrays for lists, associative arrays for key-value maps — both are essential for writing scripts that don't fall apart on filenames with spaces.

sections.title: Indexed arrays
sections.body:
**Why:** without arrays you end up doing fragile things like `PODS=$(kubectl get pods | awk '{print $1}')` and iterating over a string. When a pod name has a space (or your output has a blank line), it breaks. Arrays fix this.

```bash
# Declare and populate
pods=("argocd-server-abc" "argocd-repo-server-xyz" "argocd-redis-123")

# Access by index
echo "${pods[0]}"           # argocd-server-abc
echo "${pods[-1]}"          # last element: argocd-redis-123

# All elements
echo "${pods[@]}"           # space-separated (use in loops)
echo "${pods[*]}"           # same but respects IFS

# Length
echo "${#pods[@]}"          # 3

# Slice: elements 1 and 2
echo "${pods[@]:1:2}"

# Append
pods+=("argocd-dex-456")

# Iterate safely (handles spaces in names)
for pod in "${pods[@]}"; do
    echo "Checking: $pod"
done

# Build array from command output — readarray is the safe way
# (don't do: pods=($( kubectl get pods )) — breaks on spaces)
readarray -t pods < <(kubectl get pods -n argocd --no-headers -o custom-columns=":metadata.name")

for pod in "${pods[@]}"; do
    restarts=$(kubectl get pod "$pod" -n argocd -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount}')
    echo "$pod: $restarts restarts"
done

# Delete element
unset 'pods[1]'

# Delete whole array
unset pods
```

sections.title: Associative arrays (dictionaries)
sections.body:
**Why:** when you need to map one thing to another — namespace to cost, pod to status, env to kubecontext — associative arrays beat parallel arrays or repeated grep.

```bash
# Must declare explicitly
declare -A context_map

context_map["prod"]="eks-prod-mach-x7kq"
context_map["staging"]="eks-staging"
context_map["dev"]="minikube"

# Access
echo "${context_map[prod]}"

# Check if key exists
if [[ -v context_map[prod] ]]; then
    echo "prod context: ${context_map[prod]}"
fi

# All keys
echo "${!context_map[@]}"

# All values
echo "${context_map[@]}"

# Iterate
for env in "${!context_map[@]}"; do
    echo "$env -> ${context_map[$env]}"
done

# Practical: map namespaces to their ArgoCD app names
declare -A ns_to_app=(
    ["argocd"]="argocd-app"
    ["monitoring"]="monitoring-stack"
    ["harbor"]="harbor"
    ["external-secrets"]="external-secrets"
)

for ns in "${!ns_to_app[@]}"; do
    app="${ns_to_app[$ns]}"
    status=$(argocd app get "$app" -o json 2>/dev/null | jq -r '.status.sync.status // "Unknown"')
    printf "%-20s %-30s %s\n" "$ns" "$app" "$status"
done
```

sections.title: Process substitution — <() and >()
sections.body:
**Why:** sometimes you need to feed command output to something that expects a file, or compare two commands' output without temp files. Process substitution gives you a named pipe on the fly.

```bash
# <(cmd) — treat cmd's output as a file

# Compare two kubectl outputs side by side
diff <(kubectl get pods -n staging) <(kubectl get pods -n prod)

# readarray from a command (you saw this above)
readarray -t pods < <(kubectl get pods -A --no-headers | awk '{print $2}')

# while read loop without a subshell (critical difference!)
# BAD: runs in subshell, variable changes are lost after loop
kubectl get pods | while read -r line; do
    count=$((count + 1))  # count is lost after the pipe
done

# GOOD: process substitution keeps variables in current shell
count=0
while IFS= read -r line; do
    count=$((count + 1))
done < <(kubectl get pods -A --no-headers)
echo "Total pods: $count"  # works!

# >(cmd) — feed output of a command into another command as a file
# tee to two different processors at once
kubectl get pods -A -o json | tee >(jq '.items | length' > /tmp/pod-count.txt) | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.name'

# Join two sorted lists
join <(sort file1.txt) <(sort file2.txt)
```

sections.title: Advanced patterns: nameref, mapfile, indirect expansion
sections.body:
```bash
# nameref — reference another variable by name (bash 4.3+)
declare -n ref=myvar
myvar="hello"
echo "$ref"   # hello — ref IS myvar
ref="world"
echo "$myvar" # world

# Useful for passing array names to functions
process_list() {
    local -n items=$1   # nameref to the array passed by name
    for item in "${items[@]}"; do
        echo "Processing: $item"
    done
}

my_pods=("pod-a" "pod-b" "pod-c")
process_list my_pods   # pass array by name, not by value

# mapfile / readarray — read lines into array
mapfile -t namespaces < <(kubectl get namespaces -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}' | tr ' ' '\n')

# mapfile with transformation (-C callback every N lines)
mapfile -t -C 'echo "Read line:"' -c 1 lines < /etc/hosts

# Indirect expansion — variable whose value is another variable's name
ENV=prod
prod_context="eks-prod-mach-x7kq"
var_name="${ENV}_context"
echo "${!var_name}"   # eks-prod-mach-x7kq

# Practical: select kubeconfig based on ENV variable
for ENV in prod staging dev; do
    context_var="${ENV}_context"
    declare "${ENV}_context"="eks-${ENV}"
done
echo "${!prod_context}"  # eks-prod... wait, this gets tricky fast
# Prefer associative arrays for this case
```

sections.title: Cheat sheet
sections.body:
```bash
# ── Indexed arrays ──────────────────────────────
arr=(a b c)              # declare
arr+=(d)                 # append
${arr[0]}                # first element
${arr[-1]}               # last element
${arr[@]}                # all elements (use in loops)
${#arr[@]}               # length
${arr[@]:1:2}            # slice: 2 elements starting at index 1
readarray -t arr < <(cmd) # safe: populate from command
for x in "${arr[@]}"; do  # safe iteration

# ── Associative arrays ───────────────────────────
declare -A map
map[key]=value
${map[key]}              # access
${!map[@]}               # all keys
${map[@]}                # all values
[[ -v map[key] ]]        # key exists?

# ── Process substitution ─────────────────────────
diff <(cmd1) <(cmd2)     # compare two commands
while read -r x; do      # loop without subshell
  ...
done < <(cmd)
readarray -t arr < <(cmd) # populate array from cmd

# ── Common mistakes ──────────────────────────────
# WRONG: arr=($(...))    -- breaks on spaces/globs
# RIGHT: readarray -t arr < <(...)

# WRONG: cmd | while read  -- changes lost (subshell)
# RIGHT: while read; done < <(cmd)

# WRONG: for x in ${arr[@]}  -- breaks on spaces
# RIGHT: for x in "${arr[@]}"
```

sections.title: Quiz
sections.body:
Answer these before checking — think it through first.

**Q1.** What's the difference between `${arr[@]}` and `${arr[*]}`?

**Q2.** Why does `cmd | while read -r line; do count=$((count+1)); done; echo $count` print 0?

**Q3.** You have a script that receives an environment name (`prod`, `staging`) and needs to look up its kubecontext. What's the cleanest bash approach?

**Q4.** What does `readarray -t` do that plain `arr=($(cmd))` doesn't?

---

**Answers:**

**A1.** With double quotes: `"${arr[@]}"` expands each element as a separate word (safe). `"${arr[*]}"` joins all elements with the first char of IFS (usually a space) into one word.

**A2.** The `while` loop runs in a subshell (due to the pipe). Variables modified in a subshell don't persist to the parent. Fix: `while read -r line; do ...; done < <(cmd)`.

**A3.** Associative array: `declare -A ctx=([prod]=eks-prod [staging]=eks-staging)` then `${ctx[$ENV]}`.

**A4.** `readarray -t` reads each line as a separate array element and strips the trailing newline (`-t`). `arr=($(cmd))` does word-splitting on spaces AND glob-expands, breaking on filenames with spaces or special chars.

---

**Exercise:** Try this in the terminal:

```bash
# Build a namespace health map
declare -A health

readarray -t namespaces < <(kubectl get namespaces --no-headers | awk '{print $1}')

for ns in "${namespaces[@]}"; do
    bad=$(kubectl get pods -n "$ns" --no-headers 2>/dev/null \
        | grep -cv Running || true)
    health[$ns]=$bad
done

echo "Namespace health report:"
for ns in "${!health[@]}"; do
    count=${health[$ns]}
    if [[ $count -gt 0 ]]; then
        echo "  [$count issues] $ns"
    else
        echo "  [OK] $ns"
    fi
done | sort
```
